html:
Coffee came to Brazil in 1727, when the Portuguese officer Francisco de Melo Palheta brought seedlings from French Guiana to Pará. Legend says he charmed the French governor's wife, who slipped him the plants in a bouquet.

For decades coffee was a minor crop. It took off in the early 1800s in the hills around Rio de Janeiro, the Paraíba valley, then spread to São Paulo. Plantations were worked by enslaved Africans, and coffee kept the slave trade going in Brazil long after other countries had dropped it. Brazil has been the world's largest coffee producer since the 1840s.

Coffee shaped the country:

  • It made São Paulo rich, paid for railways, and gave planters great power in politics.
  • After slavery ended in 1888, it drew millions of migrants from Italy and later Japan.
  • Its prices rose and fell with the world economy, and the crash of 1929 hit Brazil hard.

Brazil still grows about a third of the world's coffee. The drink first spread from Yemen through the Muslim world and Europe.
